strengths: Addressing the reliability of segmentation systems in practice is a timely topic.
To name one, the broad topic that this paper covers, i.e. uncertainty estimation in medical imaging, is an important one.

This paper investigates the critical challenge of quantifying uncertainty in medical image segmentation powered by CNNs. The authors undertake a comprehensive exploration of potential solutions, ranging from uncertainty-sensitive fusion strategies to entropy-based uncertainty evaluation techniques. The conceptual foundation is robust, and the approach is astutely anchored in established prior works.

The introduced test-time augmentation, when amalgamated with EUA, consistently outshines several benchmarks. This accomplishment not only sets a commendable precedent but also furnishes valuable insights that can pave the way for subsequent research.
weaknesses: The method of running Monte Carlo Dropout at test time and computing entropy scores on the samples for uncertainty estimation in semantic segmentation is presented as a contribution (named GUE or TTD+EUA) despite being widely adopted in the community and the sections describing it are extremely similar to sections 3.1-3.5 in [1] without adequate reference.

Much of the text in Section 2.1 describing the URF technique is very similar to Section III in [8] (again no reference), and it is unclear how the proposed URF differs from the uncertainty-aware ensemble boosting in [8].

It is unclear what the actual purpose of the URF method is; the paper suggests it is meant to improve calibration, but the term “calibration” is not mentioned in the main paper and no reasoning is given for why URF should improve pixel‑wise calibration or why such calibration matters for segmentation systems.

Evidence that URF improves pixel‑wise calibration would require comparison against actual calibration methods, but the paper lacks such baselines; the methods listed in Table 1 (Pappagari, Sarawgi, Rohanian) are never introduced outside the table and none are proposed or tested for calibration, and simple temperature scaling baselines are missing.

The validated regression task reported in Tables 1 and 2 (measured by RMSE/MPIW/PICP) is surprising because no actual regression task is described; the use‑case based on the MURA dataset is presented as classification of fractures, not regression.
Overall, there is little information about the goals and reasoning behind URF, as the rest of the paper discusses unrelated techniques (TTD/EUA/GUE/VVC).

Much of the evaluation in the Appendix focuses on Dice score improvements from TTD/EUA or different segmentation backbones (e.g., V‑Net) without comparison to the state‑of‑the‑art medical segmentation method nnU‑Net [9], making the improvements unconvincing.

Essential sections such as experimental setup, related work, and task definition are either missing entirely or moved to the Appendix, rendering the main paper unreadable without the Appendix and giving an unfair advantage over other ICLR submissions.

The paper creates considerable confusion, appearing stitched together from various sources; there is no clear task definition, with mentions of categorization, classification, regression, segmentation, and calibration presented inconsistently throughout the text.
Anonymity is breached several times, for example by referring to "our MURA data set" and revealing the affiliation of employed radiologists.
Appendix A introduces Cohen’s kappa metric, but this metric is never used later in the paper.
A “Grand Challenge 4” is mentioned in the Summary without any context or reference.
The heading “Fluky Model” appears in 2.2.1 but the term is never mentioned again.
The proposed method URF_w is never introduced or defined.
Calibration baselines in Table 1 (Pappagari, Sarawgi, Rohanian) are never introduced or described.
The technique of computing entropy scores based on Monte Carlo dropout is first called GUE and later TTD+EUA, causing inconsistency.
Section 2.2 appears to be about test‑time augmentations (as in [1]) but this is never mentioned in the paper.
Figure 1 is said to illustrate the methods VF, URF, and URF_w, but it does not actually do so.
The described problem/motivation (addressing batch effects) is never explicitly addressed in the presented work.

The application is too specific for ICLR: the paper makes general methodological claims yet only studies 2D segmentation of musculoskeletal radiographs, whereas diversity of medical datasets requires evaluation on many datasets.
Even if technical novelty, presentation, and evaluation issues were fixed, the work would still not be suitable for publication at ICLR.
The whole writing in the paper is very vague and superficial; the abstract and introduction lack concrete ideas and clear context for the claimed contributions.
No experiments are provided in the main text; experiments are only in the appendix, disconnected from the main text and lacking a clear experimental setting.
The methodological contribution URF is described vaguely; the problem formulation is poorly described, and novelty is hard to evaluate because related work is not discussed in detail.
Figure 1 is claimed to illustrate VF, URF, and URF_w, but the figure’s caption and content do not describe these three approaches.
Some sentences lack coherence, such as the lengthy sentence in section 2.1 describing Vanilla Fusion (VF) and its loss weighting.
It would be helpful to clarify what “modality” refers to; the paper focuses solely on CNN‑driven medical image segmentation despite mentioning multimodalities.

The authors should discuss prior works on test‑time augmentation more thoroughly (e.g., the study at https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-020-61808-3) and highlight how the proposed TTA improves upon previous approaches.

The structure of the paper could be improved: readers must refer to the appendix for the experiment section, numerous typos are present, and the overall layout does not meet high‑quality writing standards, necessitating a significant revision.
